overview.title: 📖 Overview: Value, Substitution, and Whose Offering Is It?
overview.subtitle: Keritot 27a–27b
overview.hebrewSource: אָדָם מִתְכַּפֵּר בִּשְׁבַח הֶקְדֵּשׁ, אוֹ לֹא
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf resolves the previous daf's terminology puzzle about 'his misuse' before turning to a foundational question: if a consecrated animal's market value rises while in the owner's possession, can he use that appreciation toward his offering, or must the offering's value match the amount originally designated? Several proof attempts are tested and rejected before a baraita settles the matter. Rabbi Elazar then raises this same dilemma independently, prompting Rabbi Yoḥanan's surprise that his own student hadn't already absorbed the answer — a pattern repeated with two more of Rabbi Elazar's dilemmas, about permanently disqualified sacred animals and about offerings when market prices shift. The daf's second half turns to two new mishnayot: one establishing that a son can never bring his deceased father's designated sin offering, nor may anyone redirect an offering from one sin to another, and another detailing exactly how a person may substitute between sliding-scale offering tiers as his financial circumstances change.

slides.title: 📈 Can a Person Achieve Atonement with Appreciated Value?
slides.subtitle: Rav Menashya bar Gadda's dilemma about accumulated one-fifth payments

lines.speaker: The dilemma
lines.text: If someone accumulates enough one-fifth misuse payments to total two sela, can he use that sum to purchase a guilt offering and achieve atonement — the same way an animal that grows more valuable while in his possession might count?

lines.speaker: Attempted proofs
lines.text: Several mishnayot and baraitot are tested: a ram bought cheap that appreciated on its own; a ram deliberately FATTENED (where the owner invested effort and expense); each time, the Gemara distinguishes whether the added value came from the owner's own exertion or merely happened passively

lines.speaker: Conclusion
lines.text: A baraita settles it: 'worth one sela at designation, two sela at the time of atonement — he has NOT fulfilled his obligation.' Passive appreciation does not count.

callout.label: Why it matters:
callout.text: The distinction between effort-driven value increase (fattening) and passive market appreciation determines whether many real-world scenarios of accumulating small sums toward an offering are valid.

slides.title: ❓ Rabbi Elazar's Puzzling Dilemmas
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yoḥanan's astonishment — and where these questions actually lead
slides.hebrewSource: כַּמָּה שָׁנִים גָּדַל זֶה בֵּינֵינוּ, וְלֹא שָׁמַע הֲלָכָה זוֹ מִמֶּנִּי
slides.label: The pattern:
slides.text: Three times, Rabbi Elazar raises a dilemma to Rabbi Yoḥanan — the same 'appreciated value' question independently; whether permanently disqualified living consecrated animals (ba'alei ḥayim nidḥin) can ever become fit again; and what happens if lamb prices crash so low that a fixed two-sela guilt offering becomes unobtainable. Each time, Rabbi Yoḥanan expresses genuine surprise that his own student hadn't already absorbed these answers from years of study together. The Gemara traces each answer to teachings Rabbi Yoḥanan HAD given, just not in direct response to these exact dilemmas — for instance, a partnership-consecration case yields three halakhot at once, including that disqualification can indeed be permanent. But the third dilemma, about depreciated lamb prices, ends unresolved: Abaye and Rava each raise counter-cases (an ordinary sin offering; a nazirite's 'offering that comes for naught') that seem to contradict the proposed reasoning, and the Gemara simply concludes: 'this is difficult' (קַשְׁיָא).

slides.title: 👨‍👦 A Son Cannot Bring His Father's Sin Offering
slides.subtitle: A new mishna's rule, unpacked through a chain of verse-based exclusions
rows: Son brings father's already-designated ANIMAL for a different-severity sin
'His offering' (Lev. 4:23) — must be his own
Son brings father's designated animal even for an EQUALLY severe sin
'His offering' repeated (Lev. 4:28) — no exception for matching severity
Son uses father's designated MONEY (not yet an animal) for his own offering
Contrast with nazirite law, where unallocated money CAN pass to an heir — sin offering money cannot
A person redirects his OWN designated offering from one sin to a different one
'His offering for HIS sin' — must match the specific sin, even if equally severe

callout.label: The animal/money distinction:
callout.text: Redirecting a designated ANIMAL to a different sin fails entirely (no misuse, no atonement — it simply can't be reassigned); but redirecting designated MONEY does constitute misuse of consecrated property, since money, unlike an already-designated animal, can still be legally redirected via that specific mechanism.

slides.title: 🔄 Deriving 'From His Sin' and 'Concerning His Sin'
slides.subtitle: Why the Torah uses two different phrases for different tiers of the sliding-scale offering

steps.content: 1️⃣ 'From his sin' (מֵחַטָּאתוֹ) appears for both the lamb/goat tier AND the bird tier — teaching that money designated for one can be REDIRECTED, even partially, to the other as wealth changes

2️⃣ Without this phrase appearing for BIRDS specifically, one might think money designated for a bird pair couldn't convert to flour when the person becomes even poorer — since flour isn't a 'blood offering' like lamb/bird are

3️⃣ 'Concerning his sin' (עַל חַטָּאתוֹ), used specifically for the flour tier, teaches the OPPOSITE movement — that money designated for flour must be ADDED TO (not simply reassigned) when the person becomes wealthier, since flour is a different category of offering entirely

4️⃣ Together, the two phrases map the full bidirectional flow: redirect freely between lamb/goat and bird (both blood offerings), but ADD to move up from flour, and simply switch categories to move down to flour

callout.label: Precision matters:
callout.text: Every phrase's specific wording — not just its general meaning — is mined to establish the exact mechanics of converting between offering tiers.

slides.title: 🐑 Moving Between Tiers as Wealth Changes
slides.subtitle: A new mishna: exactly how the sliding-scale offering adjusts to shifting finances
rows: Money for a lamb or goat
Becomes poorer
Bring a bird instead (leftover money becomes non-sacred)
Money for a lamb or goat
Becomes even poorer
Bring one-tenth ephah of flour
Money for one-tenth ephah of flour
Becomes wealthier
Add money, bring a bird
Money for one-tenth ephah of flour
Becomes even wealthier
Add money, bring a lamb or goat
A lamb/goat itself develops a blemish
N/A
Redeem it, use proceeds toward a bird — but a BIRD that develops a blemish has no redemption at all, since birds cannot be redeemed

callout.label: Bottom line:
callout.text: The system allows fluid downward substitution (freely) and upward substitution (by adding funds), but a disqualified bird offering has no path to conversion — its money is simply lost to that specific purpose.

summary.principle: Whether appreciated value counts toward an offering, whether a father's or one's own misdirected designation can ever be repurposed, and exactly how sliding-scale offerings convert between tiers are all governed by the Torah's precise wording — down to the specific choice between 'from his sin' and 'concerning his sin.'

flowSteps.content: 📈 A consecrated animal's passive appreciation in value does not count toward fulfilling an offering obligation
❓ Rabbi Elazar's three dilemmas test the edges of consecration law, with mixed and sometimes unresolved results
👨‍👦 A father's designated sin offering — animal or money — can never pass to his son, nor can one's own offering be redirected between different sins

columns.content: 🔄 'From his sin' and 'concerning his sin' each license a different direction of tier-substitution
🐑 A new mishna maps the practical mechanics of moving between lamb/goat, bird, and flour offerings

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: even the choice between two near-synonymous prepositions in the Torah's text carries distinct, deliberate halakhic weight

quiz.q: According to the baraita that settles Rav Menashya bar Gadda's dilemma, if an animal was worth one sela when designated as a guilt offering but appreciated to two sela by the time of sacrifice, has the owner fulfilled his obligation?
o: Yes, since the offering is now worth the required amount
No — passive appreciation in value does not count toward fulfilling the obligation
Yes, but only if he actively cared for the animal
The mishna leaves this unresolved
quiz.e: The baraita explicitly rules that one has NOT fulfilled his obligation in this case, establishing that mere passive appreciation in a consecrated animal's value does not count toward the required offering value.

quiz.q: What was Rabbi Yoḥanan's reaction each time Rabbi Elazar raised one of his dilemmas?
o: He praised Rabbi Elazar's originality
He expressed surprise that his own student hadn't already learned the answer from him after so many years of study
He refused to answer
He said the questions were unimportant
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan responded each time with astonishment, noting how many years Rabbi Elazar had studied with him without having already absorbed the relevant halakha.

quiz.q: According to the mishna and its derivation, why can a son never fulfill his own sin-offering obligation using an animal his deceased father had already designated, even for an identical transgression?
o: Because sons are exempt from all sin offerings
Because the verse 'his offering' (repeated in Leviticus 4:23 and 4:28) teaches that one fulfills his obligation only with his OWN offering, never his father's, regardless of matching severity
Because animals cannot be inherited
Because only money, never animals, can be inherited for this purpose
quiz.e: The doubled phrase 'his offering' is expounded to exclude even the case of matching severity between father's and son's sin, establishing that one can never fulfill his obligation with an offering designated by someone else, even a parent.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's explanation, what is the key difference between redirecting an already-designated ANIMAL to a different sin versus redirecting designated MONEY to a different sin?
o: There is no difference between them

Redirecting an animal fails entirely (no misuse occurs and no atonement results), while redirecting money constitutes actual misuse of consecrated property and can achieve atonement through that mechanism
Money can never be redirected under any circumstances
Animals can always be redirected freely
quiz.e: The Gemara distinguishes that an already-designated animal simply cannot be repurposed for a different sin at all, whereas money, if misdirected, triggers the halakhot of misuse of consecrated property, which can itself provide a path to atonement.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, what happens if someone designates a bird pair as a sliding-scale sin offering and the bird then develops a blemish?
o: He redeems the bird and brings flour instead
He may not bring one-tenth of an ephah of flour with the bird's value, since birds cannot be redeemed at all
He simply brings another bird for free
The blemish has no effect on the offering
quiz.e: The mishna specifically states that a blemished bird cannot be converted toward a flour offering, since unlike animals, birds have no mechanism of redemption — the money designated for that bird simply cannot be repurposed this way.
